prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: I opened with the Higgs discovery (B056) because it is the most sharply defined discovery on the list, and I still hold that view of its science. But the committee's job is to identify the discovery first and the people second, and on that test the optical lattice clock (B008) is the strongest case we can actually write down today. It is a concrete invention with a clear before and after: magic-wavelength trapping removes Doppler and recoil shifts while interrogating many atoms at once, taking fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. It is independently reproduced across Sr, Yb and Hg in many laboratories, it underpins the planned redefinition of the second, and it enables tests of fundamental constants and relativistic geodesy. The credit is also unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for driving it to record accuracy and many-body-enhanced operation. Every one of the eight members ranked it, and four put it first or second. That breadth is not merit in itself, but it tells me the scientific case survives scrutiny from theorists, atomic physicists and experimentalists alike, which is not true of my own first choice.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes. Frequency-comb technology (2005) and the control of single trapped ions (2012) are the precursors, and Ye in particular trained in the comb tradition, so a sceptic can call the lattice clock an excellent refinement of recognised work. There is also a genuine priority question between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstrations, and other groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE and Tokyo contributed to the ecosystem. I also note that my own preference for B056 is not refuted by this: the Higgs observation is arguably the larger scientific event, and a clock prize should not displace it merely because it is easier to attribute. The difficulty with B056 is attribution to individuals inside two huge collaborations, not the discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B008 first, arguing that the lattice clock is a decisive improvement in what can be measured, that it is mature and reproduced by many groups, and that the surrounding comb and ion-clock work is already honoured or separable.
responses.response: I agree on the science and on the pair Katori and Ye. I do not think 'already honoured or separable' fully answers the novelty objection, though: the committee will have to say in the citation why the lattice architecture is a distinct invention and not a continuation of 2005 and 2012. I would build the citation around the lattice concept itself and avoid language that sounds like a prize for precision timekeeping generally. I also take note of your disclosed link to the Hall laboratory; it does not change my reading of the evidence, but it is a reason to record the disclosure in the minutes.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B008 first and judged the atomic-structure side, magic wavelengths and systematic shifts, to be sound, treating the relation to the comb and ion-clock prizes as a framing point rather than an obstacle.
responses.response: Your assessment of the atomic physics is the one I cannot make myself, so I rely on it. Where I am slightly more cautious is on calling the overlap only a framing point; it is the objection a sceptical member of the Academy would raise first. I think it is answerable, because the lattice clock introduced a new route to many-atom, Doppler-free interrogation that neither the comb nor single-ion control provides, but the committee should say so explicitly. I would not accept a configuration that tries to widen the credit to comb or ultrastable-laser contributors to settle the matter.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B008 first and B042 (IceCube) second, valuing B008 as a measurement capability with broad downstream use and noting that IceCube opened neutrino astronomy but leaves attribution among IceCube, AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND unresolved.
responses.response: We agree on B008 and on IceCube as a serious runner-up, which I also ranked third. I share your concern that a Halzen and Karle prize leaves real allocation questions open. Where we differ a little is weight: I would treat the discovery of the diffuse flux as scientifically the more consequential event, and the source identifications are still maturing, so I would hold IceCube back for a later year rather than force it now. If the committee wants a second part, I would sooner see it be the Higgs experimental discovery than IceCube, though I recognise that three-name limit makes this awkward.

responses.point: Olsson ranked the spherical-aberration corrector (B009) first and B008 second, calling the corrector a clear invention with a concrete before-and-after, while noting that Krivanek's STEM work lies outside the credited names.
responses.response: I take the instrument-invention argument seriously, and it is close in kind to the lattice clock. My reservation is that the credit problem you yourself identify for the correctors, with independent TEM and STEM developments, is sharper than for B008, where two named people carry most of the decisive contribution. That is why I place B008 above it. I would not dismiss B009, but a prize that must leave out Krivanek is harder to defend than one that credits Katori and Ye.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Exact priority between the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations, which I recall from memory and have not verified.

Whether the Higgs experimental discovery (B056) can be credited to three of its four named people without distorting the collaborative record, and whether a two-part prize is preferable to a single part.
Whether the committee has an appetite for a further precision-measurement prize given recent awards in neighbouring areas.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none is connected to the optical lattice clock candidate or the named alternatives.
